title: How Should We Teach Students to Interpret Texts?
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau confesses to a mistake he made for years as an English teacher: treating independent interpretation as something to be practiced into existence, when it is actually the end product of accumulated literary knowledge, not a teachable generic skill. He diagnoses the root error as 'expertise induced blindness' — experienced readers have automatized their pattern-matching so thoroughly that interpretation feels like a free-floating skill, when in fact every connection they make (his example: a student linking Orwell's 1984 to a Doors lyric) depends entirely on knowledge the student happens to already possess. Didau argues this default 'what do you think of this?' approach is inadvertently elitist, since it silently rewards students who arrive with the most literary and cultural background and offers nothing to those who don't. His proposed alternative sequences explicit teaching of competing interpretations before withdrawing guidance: teach one text-supported reading, teach a contradictory text-supported reading, have students judge between them, and only gradually move toward independent interpretation once students have internalized a repertoire of interpretive patterns. He frames the underlying goal as 'gapless instruction' — never asking students to perform a complex interpretive act without first ensuring they have the component knowledge it depends on — concluding that real independence in interpretation 'rests on internalised knowledge,' not on repeated practice at guessing.
points: Didau's diagnosis of 'expertise induced blindness' — where expert readers mistake their automatized, knowledge-dependent pattern-matching for a generic transferable skill — reframes a common English-teaching failure mode as a specific cognitive bias rather than a simple pedagogical oversight.

His claim that the default 'what do you think?' approach is 'inadvertently elitist' because it rewards students who arrive with the most literary and cultural resources gives the piece an equity argument that goes beyond pure pedagogy.

The explicit five-step sequence — teach one interpretation, teach a contradictory interpretation, have students judge between them, teach that validity depends on textual support, then gradually withdraw guidance — offers English teachers a concrete alternative to open-ended discussion that still ends in genuine independent interpretation.
quotes: My problem was that I'd confused independence as an educational aim with independence as a teaching method. I wanted students to become independent interpreters and assumed the best way to achieve this was to get them interpreting independently. But independence is the product of expertise not a mechanism for acquiring it.

As experts, we've automatised the pattern matching involved in interpretation. Because this is what we think happens in our own heads, we believe that if only we can teach students the skill of interpreting, they'll be fine. This, however, is a classic case of expertise induced blindness.
It's not that interpretation isn't skilful, it's that the skill can't usefully be separated from the knowledge that makes it possible. The more we know, the better we are at interpreting texts.

All too often, our approach is inadvertently elitist. An approach intended to promote independence can privilege precisely those students who arrived with the greatest literary and cultural resources.

The goal here is 'gapless instruction'. Every time we rely on knowledge we haven't taught, or ask students to perform a complex process without ensuring they possess its component knowledge, we create a gap.
Genuine independence rests on internalised knowledge. If our goal is to teach children to interpret independently we must give them enough knowledge to think with.
